summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is a web app that turns NASA climate data into a clear answer to four questions: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically real.

It analyses three NASA datasets: surface temperature (GISTEMP v4, since 1880), and snow depth and precipitation (NASA POWER / MERRA-2, since 1981). The user picks an indicator, season, period and region. The app computes the trend for every grid cell and for the whole region, using the Theil–Sen slope and the Mann–Kendall test, with an optional false-discovery-rate correction.

Results appear as a global trend map, a yearly time series, a comparison of two regions and a ranking of regions. A plain-language finding states the rate per decade and whether it is significant: for example, Central Asia has warmed by 0.31 °C per decade since 1950, about twice the global rate of 0.16 °C. The analysis exports to PDF, Word or CSV.

Climate claims are often made without showing whether a trend is distinguishable from noise. This tool makes that check visible to students, journalists and local planners: insignificant trends are washed out on the map and labelled as such, rather than presented as findings. It is also open about its sources: snow and precipitation come from model reanalysis, not direct observations.
details:
What Earth System Trend Detective Does
Earth System Trend Detective is a web application that turns NASA climate data into a plain answer to four questions: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically real. The user chooses an indicator (surface temperature, snow depth or precipitation), a season, a period of ten years or more and a region — one of ten presets or any rectangle on the map. The app returns a global trend map, a yearly time series, a comparison of two regions, a ranking of regions and a one-sentence finding in plain language. Every result can be exported as a PDF or Word report, or as CSV data.


How It Works – Key Technical Elements

Data pipeline. Monthly gridded data is downloaded directly from NASA's open servers: GISTEMP v4 for temperature (since 1880) and NASA POWER / MERRA-2 for snow depth and precipitation (since 1981). Monthly values are averaged into yearly or seasonal means; incomplete years are dropped.

Trend per grid cell. For each of up to 51,840 cells the app computes the Theil–Sen slope: the median of the slopes between all pairs of years. A single extreme year cannot distort it.

Significance test. The Mann–Kendall test decides whether the direction of change is consistent. It does not assume normally distributed data.

False discovery control. A map tests thousands of cells at once, so some would look significant by chance. An optional Benjamini–Hochberg correction keeps such false findings down.

Regional trend. The regional series is an area-weighted mean (weights proportional to the cosine of latitude), so small polar cells do not dominate.

Honest map. A cell with a significant trend is drawn in full colour; a cell with an insignificant trend is washed out. Uncertainty is visible at a glance.

Benefits and Goals
Climate charts are widely shared, but rarely with a check that the change stands out from normal year-to-year variation. NASA data is open, yet reading it takes code and statistics. Our app removes both barriers: a student, a journalist or a local planner can check a claim about their own region in under a minute, on a computer or a phone, and see how far the result can be trusted. The goal is to make "is this trend real?" as easy to answer as "what does the chart look like?".

Presenting the Results – Case Study: Tajikistan
Surface temperature, whole year, 1980–2025
Tajikistan: +0.38 °C per decade, +1.72 °C in total, p < 0.001 — statistically significant.
Global average: +0.21 °C per decade, +0.94 °C in total, p < 0.001.
The Compare view states the ratio only because both trends are significant: Tajikistan is warming 1.8 times faster than the planet.
For context, the regional ranking gives the Arctic +0.69 °C, Europe +0.47 °C, Central Asia +0.39 °C and Australia +0.17 °C per decade.
Snow depth, whole year, 1981–2025
Tajikistan: −0.15 cm per decade, p = 0.45 — not statistically significant. The app reports that the change cannot be told apart from random variation instead of presenting it as a decline.
Arctic: −0.97 cm per decade, p < 0.001 — significant.
Global land average: −0.10 cm per decade, p < 0.001, with significant change on 16% of the land area.
The two results for the same country show the purpose of the tool: it confirms a trend where the data supports one and declines to claim one where it does not.

Limitations We State Openly
Snow depth and precipitation come from the MERRA-2 reanalysis, a model constrained by observations, not from direct measurements.
The precipitation series shows a step around 2012 in some regions, which may be a data artefact. We do not present precipitation trends as findings without an independent cross-check.
The Mann–Kendall test ignores autocorrelation, so significance may be slightly overstated.
Cells where snow never melts (glaciers and ice caps) are excluded from the snow analysis, because the reanalysis does not model their mass balance.
A significant trend shows that a change is not random. It does not explain the cause.

Tools and Technologies

Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, xarray.
Frontend: Angular, TypeScript, Plotly; reports generated in the browser with jsPDF and docx.
Packaging: Docker;
